title: Basal Cell Carcinoma (BCC) of the Eyelid: Histopathology & Clinical Management
summary: A comprehensive clinical and histological guide to the most common eyelid malignancy. This poster covers the spectrum from pathognomonic 'picket-fence' palisading to advanced Hedgehog pathway inhibitors.

sections.title: Histopathological Hallmarks: The 'Big Three'
content: 1. **Basaloid Islands:** Nests or cords of small, hyperchromatic cells with high N:C ratios and scant cytoplasm.
2. **Peripheral Palisading:** Outer layer of cells arranged in a 'picket-fence' pattern, perpendicular to the nest border.
3. **Retraction (Clefting) Artifacts:** Clear spaces between tumor nests and the surrounding stroma, caused by mucin contraction during fixation.

rows: Large, well-circumscribed nests; most common form.
Narrow elongated strands/nests in a dense collagenous stroma.
Jagged, spiky nests invading deep dermis.
Presence of melanin in tumor cells/melanophages.
Deep invasion; hard to clear surgically.

sections.title: Clinical Variants & Symptoms
content: Pearly, telangiectatic nodule with 'rolled' edges.
Central ulceration ('Rodent Ulcer').
Madarosis (loss of lashes) in the area of the lesion.
Cicatricial (scar-like) plaque (Morpheaform type).
Induration (firmness) extending beyond visible margins.
Destruction of the meibomian gland orifices.

sections.title: High-Risk 'Red Flags'
content: Location: Medial Canthal Area (High risk of orbital and sinus invasion via lacrimal system).
Size: Diameter > 20mm (T2 or higher staging).
Histology: Morpheaform, Infiltrative, or Perineural invasion.
Recurrent Disease: Recurrent BCC is significantly more aggressive than primary.
Immunosuppressed Patients: Faster growth and higher metastatic potential (though overall rare).

rows: Tumor involving full-thickness eyelid or orbit.
Tumor invading brain or cranial bones.

sections.title: Biopsy & Diagnostic Workup
content: 1. Clinical photography & measurement.
2. Shave or Punch Biopsy (Avoid if total excision is possible).
3. Formalin Fixation (Standard) or fresh tissue (Mohs).
4. CT/MRI Orbit (If orbital invasion/bone destruction is suspected).
5. Lymph node palpation (Preauricular and Submandibular).

sections.title: Surgical Management Hierarchy
content: Step 1: Mohs Micrographic Surgery (MMS) - Gold standard for eyelid (tissue sparing, 99% cure rate).
Step 2: Wide Local Excision with Frozen Section Control (Standard of care if Mohs unavailable).
Step 3: Surgical Margins: 3-4mm for nodular BCC; 5-10mm for morpheaform.
Step 4: Reconstruction: Pentagonal wedge, Tenzel semi-circular flap, or Hughes/Cutler-Beard flaps.
Step 5: Orbital Exenteration (Reserved for T3/T4 extensive orbital invasion).

sections.title: Medical & Targeted Therapies
content: **Hedgehog Pathway Inhibitors:** Vismodegib (Erivedge) or Sonidegib (Odomzo) for metastatic/inoperable BCC.
**Topical Imiquimod 5%:** Only for small, superficial BCC (Non-eyelid margin).
**Radiotherapy:** Adjuvant for perineural invasion or primary for patients unfit for surgery.
**Cryotherapy:** Historically used, but poor margin control (Not recommended for eyelid).

content.explanation: 4mm margins for 4-cornered (primary nodular) lesions; 10mm (1cm) margins for 10-fold dangerous (morpheaform/recurrent) lesions.

sections.title: Recent Advances: STEVIE Trial
sections.content: The STEVIE study confirmed the long-term safety and efficacy of Vismodegib in clinical practice. It showed a 68.5% response rate in locally advanced BCC, although side effects like muscle cramps, dysgeusia (taste disturbance), and alopecia are frequent limiting factors.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls & Exam High-Yields
content: BCC is the most common eyelid tumor, but SCC is more common in patients with history of radiation or severe UV damage.
Never 'watch and wait' a lesion causing madarosis—this is pathognomonic for malignancy.
The 'pearly' border is due to the lifting of the epidermis by the underlying basaloid tumor nests.
Medial canthal BCCs have 'silent' spread through the thin bone of the lacrimal fossa into the ethmoid sinuses.
In Gorlin Syndrome, look for odontogenic keratocysts, palmar/plantar pits, and calcification of the falx cerebri.
